newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian labour force data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian labour force data.

text.p: Australian employment rose by 38,400 in January, and the unemployment rate was 8.6 percent, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.
Median forecasts had centred on a rise in January employment of 10,000 and an unemployment rate of 8.6 percent.
Forecasts for employment growth had ranged up to 17,000.
Part-time employment accounted for 34,900 of the total rise.
A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follow.
AKIS HARALBAPOPOULOS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, GIO AUSTRALIA:

"It's an encouraging number. Basically it reinforces our thinking that the economy is on the mend and we can expect to see continued employment growth. Employment's going to perform well, certainly in the second half of 1997. Money in people's hip pockets, irrespective of whether its part-time or full-time, is still money in the hip pockets, and basically 34,900 is still a lot of people in part-time work. I suspect if you get a couple more increases in total employment, even if they're in the ball park 15,000 to 20,000, I think the probability of a cut in official interest continues to diminish."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, UBS AUSTRALIA:

"It's reasonably firm, even with the breakdown between part-time and full time. It's running a lot stronger than the first part of 1996, so you are starting to get a pick-up in the annual growth rate of employment up to 1.4 percent from 0.8 percent. The net result is it should continue to take away any expectations of monetary policy easing for this cycle."
ALAN OSTER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK:

"Basically, whilst a lot of it (the jobs growth) is part time, I think it's consistent with a labour market which is showing some growth. It could well be that the unemployment rate is starting to top off and if I was a central banker looking at these numbers I would basically make sure that everything was on hold for quite a while."
SHANE OLIVER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, AMP INVESTMENTS:

"Well it's certainly a lot stronger than we would have been expecting and also what the market was expecting. At this stage though I think it's probably too early to read too much into it, but the signs do appear to be there that the labour market is gradually starting to turn around. I would probably think though after this we'll see a bit of a pull back in the February figues, but nevertheless there signs there that it is gradually starting to pick up and also when you look at the forward indicators ... there are signs there that it is stabilising and starting to pick up."
SAUL ESLAKE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANKING GROUP:

"This is bad news for those who were expecting another rate cut. However, I still have my doubts about what the data is telling us. It continues the pattern of recent months in which the growth in employment is has been disproportionately part-time. It will be interesting to see in the final labour market data later this month whether or not, as we've seen in recent months, the apparent increase in employment has been paralleled by a decline in hours worked."
RIC SIMES, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ROTHSCHILD AUSTRALIA:

"January always tends to be fairly volatile because the holidays tend to knock the seasonal adjustment process around. Notwithstanding that, it (the 38,400 employment rise) has to be regarded as a strong number and consistent with the labour market starting to look a bit better after a very weak 1996. It's also consistent with the notion that 1997 overall looks a bit stronger and there's little chance of another rate cut."
ROB HENDERSON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DRESDNER INTERNATIONAL:

"I am pretty encouraged by the growth in the trend numbers in the employment series. If you look at the trend figure in the December publication we had 8,200 jobs growth in December versus November, if you look at the trend figure for the January numbers you get 12,200. So definitely there is an acceleration going on in the trend numbers. That to me says that we are well and truly out of the woods in terms of employment growth, we have got an economy that is starting to generate jobs again. It looks like we are starting to get into a situation where jobs gwroth is strong enought to get the unemployment rate coming down. CHRIS CATON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST AUSTRALIA:

"The point does need to be stressed that almost all the employment gain was part-time. There are some seasonal things that go on in December and January, but we've had over the last half of last year, particularly when you adjust for the distortion caused by the transfer to the phone interviewing, we've apparently had a quite decent employment pick-up. So yes, I think it does vindicate his (RBA Governor Ian Macfarlane's) views (that employment was picking up)."
JOHN EDWARDS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, SOCIETE GENERALE:

"It's a very, very large number -- mostly part time of course, but that's often the case. Unless there's a trick at work which so far we have not identified, it does seem to confirm Ian Macfarlane's view that the economy is entering 1997 stronger than it left 1996 and in turn diminishes the argument for a rate cut. It's often been the case that part time employment has led total employment, both up and down, and indeed over the last decade the pattern of Australian employment has been changing towards more part time so I don't place a lot of emphasis on that or on unemployment staying up.
